turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell raised a perfectly sculpted eyebrow, regarding Mr. Worthing with a degree of skepticism that could curdle cream. Such details, she intimated, were of paramount importance in determining a gentleman’s standing.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen declared, with a delicate flutter of her eyelashes, that the possession of a family pew was, of course, absolutely essential. She added, directing her gaze pointedly at her mother, that Mr. Worthing's suitability, and indeed their entire future happiness, depended on this very detail.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell fixed Mr. Worthing with a gaze of glacial intensity, and inquired as to the deceased parents of the gentleman occupying the Belgrave Square residence. turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen insisted, with a slight tremor in her voice, that any gentleman lacking a family pew was simply not worth considering, regardless of his Belgrave Square address. turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack stammered slightly, attempting a reassuring smile, and explained that he believed his guardian, the late Mr. Hobbs of Hobart Place, had, in fact, secured a pew for him at St. Stephen’s, though he confessed he hadn't personally confirmed the arrangement. turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell observed Mr. Worthing with a chilling stillness, her lips curving into a faint, almost imperceptible smile. Lady Bracknell declared that a gentleman’s guardian exerted a profound influence upon the character of his ward, and insisted that one could not be too exacting in such matters.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack hastened to assure Lady Bracknell that Mr. Hobbs, a man of impeccable standing, was a respected solicitor, known for his diligence and, as far as he was aware, his utterly unblemished reputation. He offered a slightly nervous smile, eager to appear agreeable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing with a withering gaze, and inquired as to the precise nature of his employment, observing that whilst a gentleman might occasionally dabble in pursuits of a more artistic bent, a certain degree of financial stability was, naturally, absolutely indispensable. turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, feeling the pressure acutely, hastened to explain that he was, at present, managing the affairs of a young ward, Miss Cecily Cardew, which provided him with a modest, though entirely respectable, income. He offered a particularly earnest smile, hoping to convey an image of financial security.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing's assertions with a degree of skepticism that might have frozen a less resolute man. turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, attempting to regain some composure, hastened to explain that Miss Cardew’s family history was, regrettably, somewhat obscure, although he understood they were of good, though distant, connections. turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing’s attempt at reassurance with a distinctly unimpressed air, and inquired as to the precise nature of these 'distant connections' to which he referred, suggesting that a thorough understanding of one's ancestry was, naturally, the very bedrock of civilized society. turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, feeling increasingly flustered by the relentless questioning, hastened to assure Lady Bracknell that he was, naturally, making every effort to trace Miss Cardew’s lineage and would present her with a complete and satisfactory account as soon as possible; he expressed a sincere hope that this would prove sufficiently illuminating, though he admitted the task proved somewhat… challenging. turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing’s rather desperate assurances with a look of profound skepticism, and inquired, with the utmost gravity, as to the precise nature of these ‘diligent efforts’ to which he referred; it is, she observed, quite insufficient to merely *intend* to investigate, one must, of course, *actually* investigate, and the results, she expected, to be presented to her in a form readily digestible by a discerning mind. turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, attempting a reassuring tone, explained that his inquiries were, naturally, proceeding with the utmost diligence, and that he had already engaged the services of a reputable family researcher to assist him. turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing’s claim of employing a ‘reputable family researcher’ with a raised eyebrow, and inquired as to the gentleman's qualifications and, crucially, his social standing. turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, attempting to regain some composure, explained that the gentleman in question, Mr. William Featherstonehaugh, possessed an impeccable record and was, he believed, quite highly regarded in genealogical circles. turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Featherstonehaugh’s name with a dubious air, and inquired, with a pointed emphasis on each syllable, whether this gentleman happened to be related, in any degree whatsoever, to the notorious Mr. Cecil Featherstonehaugh, who, she understood, had been involved in a rather unpleasant incident concerning a runaway badger and a prize-winning marrow some years ago. turns.speaker: Jack

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell fixed Mr. Worthing with a gaze of glacial disapproval. opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her pleasure, stating that a man should always have an occupation and that there were too many idle men in London. She then asked him how old he was.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell commented that it was a very good age to be married and stated that she believed a man who desired to get married should know either everything or nothing, asking him which he knew.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell observed that land had ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure and that it only provided position. She then asked about a country house.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell inquired about the number of bedrooms in the country house and then asked if he had a town house.
